finding.claim: Unauthenticated POST to /settings/email reaches set_email with uid None, so the account-write sink runs without any authentication.
finding.source: Anonymous HTTP POST to /settings/email; no session required.

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None for anonymous callers, and never aborts.

finding.guards_checked: No authentication check on this path. login_optional only attaches uid and does not enforce auth. No ownership check, no CSRF token, no re-authentication. Impact depends on the set_email stub (routes.py:48-49), which is empty, so a None uid could match unintended rows (e.g. WHERE uid IS NULL).

verdict.guard_found: none. login_optional (routes.py:19-25) only sets g.uid = session.get("uid") and never aborts, so the handler change_email (routes.py:35-37) runs for anonymous callers. No ownership, CSRF, or re-authentication check is on this path. The only other guard, login_required (routes.py:8-16), is applied to change_password, not change_email.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: the POST /settings/email route at routes.py:34-35 uses @login_optional, which at routes.py:22 sets uid to None for anonymous callers without aborting, so routes.py:37 calls set_email(None, "new@example.org") unauthenticated. The set_email body at routes.py:48-49 is an empty stub, so the real impact of a None uid is unverifiable from this code, but the unauthenticated reach to the account-write call is confirmed.

finding.claim: Email change ignores request input and always writes the same constant address, a business-logic flaw that breaks account recovery.
finding.source: Any caller of /settings/email (authenticated or anonymous, see F1).

trace.note: Writes the fixed reserved domain address new@example.org for every call.

finding.guards_checked: No input is read, so there is no injection surface. No email verification or confirmation step, and no check that the user owns the new address.

verdict.guard_found: none. routes.py:29-35 wraps change_email in login_optional, which only sets g.uid from the session and never aborts, so anonymous callers reach the handler. routes.py:37 calls set_email(g.uid, "new@example.org") as a bare statement with no input read and no ownership or verification check.
verdict.reason: The handler at routes.py:36-37 writes the same fixed address for any caller, and login_optional (routes.py:19-25) never rejects anonymous requests, so nothing blocks it. Caveat: set_email at routes.py:48-49 is a `pass` stub, so in this file the write has no observable effect; the account-recovery impact holds only once set_email is implemented.

finding.claim: Any logged-in session can set the account password to the fixed value 'hunter2' without a current-password check, enabling account takeover via session theft or CSRF.
finding.source: A request carrying a valid session with a uid, sent as a POST to /settings/password (directly or via cross-site request).

trace.note: login_required checks 'uid' in session; otherwise aborts 401.

finding.guards_checked: Session authentication is enforced. No current-password or re-authentication check. No CSRF token in this file; CSRF exposure depends on the session cookie SameSite setting, which is not configured here. Modern browsers default cookies to Lax, which limits cross-site POSTs, but this is not guaranteed across browsers or configurations.

verdict.guard_found: Only login_required (routes.py:11-12) applies: it aborts 401 when "uid" is not in session, and it sets g.uid from the session (routes.py:13). No current-password or re-authentication check exists in change_password (routes.py:42-45). No CSRF token is present in this file. The SameSite cookie setting is not configured in this file, so cross-site exposure is not confirmed from this code alone.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: change_password at routes.py:41-45 is guarded only by login_required (routes.py:8-16), which checks only for a uid in the session, and it calls set_password(g.uid, "hunter2") at routes.py:44 with no current-password check, so any holder of a valid session can set that account's password to the fixed value. The attacker must already hold a victim's session or reach it cross-site, so the impact is account takeover of the session owner's account, not privilege escalation. Note that set_password is a stub (`pass` at routes.py:52-53), so the stored effect is not shown in this file; the finding concerns the handler's behavior as written.

finding.claim: A hard-coded password literal 'hunter2' is in source, violating the org policy against hard-coded credentials and serving as the fixed value used by F3.
finding.source: Source code; anyone with read access to the repo or deployed code can see the literal.
finding.sink: Literal "hunter2" passed as the new password to set_password at routes.py:44

trace.note: String literal "hunter2" embedded directly in the handler.

finding.guards_checked: None. Org policy requires credentials to come from environment variables or managed secrets. Flag explicitly per policy.

verdict.guard_found: Only login_required (routes.py:8-16, applied at routes.py:42) gates POST /settings/password. It limits who can call the handler but does not stop the "hunter2" literal from being in source, and it does not validate or replace the value passed at routes.py:44. No credential-from-env or secrets-manager lookup exists.
verdict.reason: routes.py:44 contains the literal "hunter2" passed directly to set_password, which is a hard-coded credential in source that the org policy prohibits, and no control removes it; the endpoint is reachable by any logged-in user (routes.py:42-44). The stubbed set_password at routes.py:52-53 means the runtime impact depends on the real implementation, but the policy violation holds as stated.
